column4: A secure, tranquil town receives ample provision from every direction, then ingratitude makes it taste the “garment” of hunger and fear; tranquility, provision, trial, settlement, and worn clothing converge.
Abraham asks for a secure بلد and provision, while God says the unbeliever receives brief enjoyment before being driven to the Fire, joining settlement and supplies to divergent destinations.
The command to set out light or heavy directly answers the earthward heaviness of 9:38 and makes weight no excuse for remaining fixed.
God guides to Himself whoever turns back to Him; this Godward turning immediately precedes the heart's tranquility in 13:28.
Those whose hearts become tranquil in 13:28 receive blessedness and a beautiful homecoming, so inner rest points toward final settlement.
The Garden is brought near to the God-fearing rather than remaining distant, beginning the arrival scene completed by entry in 50:34.
The promised Garden belongs to every repeatedly returning, watchful person, identifying return as the disposition of the traveler welcomed in 50:33-34.
Believing servants are told to fear their Lord and reminded that God's earth is spacious, making migration through the earth part of faithful perseverance.
When hardship touches a person he calls on God, but after a favor he claims it came through his own knowledge; God calls the favor itself a test.
The question challenges the belief that continued wealth and sons necessarily signify favor, directly exposing the error dramatized in 89:15.
What people mistake for hastened good in 23:55 is explicitly denied, separating bestowed abundance from divine approval.
The affluent claim that superior wealth and children mean they will not be punished, the same false inference from provision to honor.
The Prophet is told to answer that God expands and restricts provision as He wills, directly matching the two conditions misread in 89:15-16.
Wealth and children do not bring people near to God; faith and action, rather than possessions, determine nearness and reward.
A person tirelessly asks for good but becomes despairing when adversity touches him, exposing a soul whose state is governed by provision.
After mercy follows adversity, the person calls it his own, doubts the Hour, and assumes a fine return, combining possession, denial of the journey's end, and false confidence.
The human being is created anxiously unstable, introducing the opposed reactions to adversity and good in 70:20-21.
When harm touches him he panics, paralleling the mistaken humiliation inferred from restricted provision.
When good touches him he withholds it, joining favorable provision to the clinging refusal to release possessions.
The recipient of wealth is told to seek the Hereafter through what God gave while using his worldly share well, turning possession into provisions for the destination.
Qarun and his house are swallowed by the earth, making worldly attachment culminate in literal earthward engulfment.
After Qarun's fall, his former admirers recognize that God expands and restricts provision and that abundance did not prove favor.
The garden owner enters his possession and asserts that it will never perish, treating a temporary station as permanent settlement.
He doubts the Hour yet assumes that, if returned to his Lord, he will find an even better destination, corrupting return into entitlement.
The garden's produce is destroyed and its owner wrings his hands over what he spent, visibly wearing away what he thought securely his.
The tested owners' garden becomes like a dark, harvested field overnight, making the attrition announced in 68:17 visible.
The owners finally confess that they have been deprived, discovering through loss that possession and provision were never guaranteed.

Abraham settles descendants in an uncultivated valley, asks that hearts incline toward them, and asks for provision, joining settlement, attachment, and sustenance without confusing any with the final home.
Those who denied meeting God arrive suddenly at the Hour carrying their burdens on their backs, turning the journey's figurative load into a final visible weight.
No burdened soul bears another's load, even a heavily laden person cannot transfer it, and the verse ends by naming God as the destination.
No burden-bearer carries another's burden, establishing the personal load whose corresponding effort is named in 53:39.
A human being has only what he strives for, closely paralleling the strenuous movement toward the Lord in 84:6.
Each person's striving will be seen, so no stage of the journey's labor disappears at arrival.
The seen striving is fully repaid before 53:42 names the Lord as the final limit.
Those who strive toward God are promised guidance along His ways, joining exertion, direction, and divine accompaniment.
“Flee to God” turns return into urgent directed motion and identifies God Himself as refuge and destination.
Believers are commanded to race toward forgiveness and a Garden, giving the final abode the force of a destination actively approached.
The command to race toward forgiveness and the Garden casts faithful life as a contest whose finish is divine pardon and abode.
Every soul is told to inspect what it has sent ahead for tomorrow, making deeds advance provisions to the destination before the traveler arrives.
Whoever wants the immediate life receives only what God wills and then reaches Hell, showing worldly preference determining a ruinous endpoint.
Whoever wants the Hereafter, strives toward it properly, and believes has that striving accepted, supplying the positive route opposite 17:18.
The person who fears standing before the Lord restrains the self from desire, reversing the worldly preference described in 79:38.
The Garden becomes the shelter of the desire-restraining traveler, completing the alternative destination to 79:39.
Angels descend upon the steadfast, remove fear and grief, and announce the promised Garden, a close communal parallel to the tranquil soul's final welcome.
The greatest terror does not grieve the faithful; angels receive them with the announcement that this is their promised day.
The God-fearing are gathered to the Merciful as an honored delegation, a dignified caravan that sharpens the companies driven to the Garden.
Criminals are driven thirsty to Hell, providing the opposed caravan and destination to the delegation in 19:85.
The God-fearing are promised a beautiful homecoming, naming the quality of the destination before its doors appear in 38:50.
Everlasting gardens stand with their gates opened to the arriving God-fearing, paralleling the opened-gate entry in 39:73.
The Garden's people suffer no fatigue and are never expelled, so arrival ends both weariness and further forced travel.
Those abiding in Paradise desire no transfer from it, explicitly marking the destination as the end of relocation.
The slain believer is directly told to enter the Garden, a singular death-side welcome closely parallel to the soul's command in surah 89.
The recipient of the right-hand record enters a “pleasing life,” echoing the root of the pleased soul at arrival.
That pleasing life is located in a lofty Garden, supplying the abode for the satisfaction named in 69:21.
The arrivals eat and drink because of what they sent ahead in past days, presenting final provision as the fruit of advance preparation.
Radiant faces are pleased with their striving, joining arduous effort to satisfaction at its result.
Those pleased with their striving in 88:9 are in a lofty Garden, locating that satisfaction at the journey's end.
God addresses prodigal people as “My servants” and forbids despair, opening a return while the journey can still change.
The servants are commanded to turn back to their Lord and submit before punishment arrives, the timely counterpart to the denied request in 23:99.
When judgment's interpretation arrives, deniers ask either for intercessors or to be returned so they can act differently, another too-late attempt to reverse the route.
The inhabitants of the Fire cry to be taken out so they can act rightly, but their completed lifespan and warning make the requested new journey unavailable.
After confessing two deaths and two lives, the condemned ask whether there is any path out, explicitly seeking a road away from the final destination.
When wrongdoers see punishment they ask whether there is any way of return, a final search for a road back after arrival.
At the coming of death, a person asks for a short delay in order to give and become righteous, seeking extra travel-time only at the endpoint.
God never delays a soul when its appointed time arrives, closing the extension requested in 63:10.
The condemned wish for one more return so they could become believers, stating the impossible repeated journey in a single request.
God sends the she-camel itself as a test, unexpectedly joining the section's camel image to its explicit theme of trial.
Shackles reaching to the chins hold rejecters with heads forced up, giving the section's binding image a scene of bodily immobilization.
God could efface their eyes so they race blindly for the path and cannot see it; 36:67 then removes even their power to advance or return.
Believers who sit without disability are not equal to those who strive with wealth and lives, making grounded nonmovement morally legible without condemning the unable.
Believers are explicitly told not all to set out; some remain to learn and warn their people, setting a boundary between necessary staying and earthbound refusal.
When God returns the Prophet to some who stayed behind, they are barred from future departure because they chose sitting the first time.
When commanded to believe and strive, the affluent ask permission to remain with those who sit, specifying privilege as a source of grounded refusal.
When mercy is withdrawn after being tasted, the human being becomes despairing and ungrateful, one half of the unstable reading of trial.
When favor follows adversity, the person exults that troubles have left and becomes boastful, completing the fortune-governed response begun in 11:9.
When warning is forgotten, every door of abundance is opened until people rejoice, then they are seized suddenly; provision functions as concealed testing.
God afflicts towns that rejected prophets with hardship so they might humble themselves, making constriction an invitation rather than proof of humiliation.
God replaces adversity with prosperity before seizing the heedless, so both conditions reveal rather than certify divine approval.
Those who desire worldly life and adornment may receive the full return of their deeds within it, but that payment does not make it the final abode.
The world-seekers of 11:15 have only Fire in the Hereafter, exposing the destination hidden by complete worldly payment.
The Prophet is told to turn from one who wants only the nearer life, identifying exclusive worldly desire as a refusal of further direction.
Seeking the Hereafter's harvest increases it, while seeking the world's harvest yields a portion with no share in the Hereafter; desire selects what the journey produces.
God carries Adam's children on land and sea and provides good things, framing human mobility and supplies as conferred honor rather than ownership.
Travelers in a ship call sincerely on God in danger, then associate partners after He delivers them to land, so safe ground becomes the place of renewed forgetfulness.
Some people travel through the earth seeking God's bounty, a direct Qur'anic instance of the country-crossing traveler whose road is tied to provision.
After creation and death, some people are returned to decrepit age, making bodily life itself a wearing process rather than a secure possession.
God creates from weakness, grants strength, then returns strength to weakness and gray age, describing the traveler's embodied arc as renewed attrition.
Whoever is granted long life is reversed in creation, a bodily counterpart to the mount and garment worn through continued use.
Humanity is created in toil, supporting the section's presentation of mortal life as an arduous passage rather than settled ease.
When one task is finished, the addressee is told to continue laboring, keeping exertion continuous until its orientation is named in 94:8.
Desire is directed toward the Lord after renewed labor in 94:7, assigning the traveler's effort its proper end.
The patient are rewarded with a lofty chamber and received there with greeting and peace, another final welcome after endurance.
Their dwelling is permanent and praised as both settlement and residence, distinguishing arrival from a temporary stop.
Patience is rewarded with a Garden and silk, allowing the source section's worn mount and garment to end in enduring shelter and clothing.
God is pleased with the faithful and they are pleased with Him, and they are named God's party, extending mutual satisfaction beyond solitary feeling into belonging.
Pharaoh's wife asks her Lord to build her a house near Him in the Garden, defining final settlement by nearness to the Lord rather than earthly palace.
On the true Day, whoever wills is invited to take a homeward course toward the Lord, expressing destination as a route deliberately chosen.
God guides the human being to the way and leaves gratitude or ingratitude as the response, joining direction to the trial of received gifts.
On the great emergence a person remembers what he strove for, bringing the whole road's effort into awareness before the two destinations are disclosed.
The one whose destination is Fire is first identified by transgression, supplying the moral movement behind the worldly preference of 79:38.
The person with heavy scales enters a pleasing life, a further use of satisfaction for the state reached after judgment.
